title: Effect of martensite pre-quenching on bainite transformation kinetics, martensite/bainite duplex microstructures, mechanical properties and retained austenite stability of GCr15 bearing steel
abstract: In this work, effect of martensite pre-quenching on the subsequent bainite transformation kinetics of GCr15 bearing steel has been investigated by means of dilatometry. The results show that the pre-quenched martensite is significantly accelerate nucleation of subsequent bainite transformation in comparison with direct bainite austempering. Meanwhile, specimen of martensite pre-quenching at 200 °C has the shortest incubation period of bainite transformation at 240 °C. Moreover, the transformation rate of bainite transformation after martensite pre-quenching is faster than direct bainite austempering in the initial growth stage, and decrease with the decreasing of martensite pre-quenching temperature. Compared with the conventional quenched and tempered (QT) specimen, the tensile strength is slightly decrease from 2170 MPa to 2143 MPa, but the impact toughness is obviously increase from 43 J to 71 J in specimen heat-treated by martensite pre-quenching at 200 °C and subsequent bainite transformation at 240 °C. In addition, the mechanical stability of retained austenite in all martensite pre-quenching specimens are higher than that of QT specimen.
journal: Journal of Materials Research and Technology

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: GCr15 bearing steel is the most commonly used material for ball and roller bearings because of its low cost and high hardenability [ 1 ]. The microstructures produced by conventional quenched and tempered (QT) heat treatment were consist of tempered martensite, retained austenite (RA) and undissolved spherical carbides which is usually cannot afford extreme loading conditions due to lower toughness, e.g., shock loads [ 2 ]. Meanwhile, GCr15 bearing steel is not suitable for use austempering treatment (isothermal holding at above martensite start (Ms) temperature) to obtain fully lower bainite microstructure due to kinetics constraints and lower strength, although lower bainite has higher toughness [ 3 , 4 ]. Therefore, the good combination of strength-toughness of GCr15 bearing steel is an urgent issue for further improve reliability and fatigue life of bearings [ 5 , 6 ].

It is well known that martensite-bainite duplex microstructures have better combination of strength-toughness than single martensite or fully lower bainite microstructures [ 7 , 8 ]. The traditional way to obtain martensite-bainite duplex microstructures in GCr15 bearing steel is by interrupt austempering process, which is first produce bainite at above Ms temperature and following form marteniste during cooling to room temperature [ 9 ]. Recently, two strategies were used to obtain martensite-bainite duplex microstructures by introduce a certain fraction of pre-quenched martensite prior to bainite transformation, one is isothermal holding below Ms temperature [ 10–12 ], the other is first martensite pre-quenching at below Ms temperature to form a certain fraction of pre-quenched martensite and following isothermal holding at above Ms temperature to produce lower bainite [ 13–15 ]. Most of current studies are focus on the effect of pre-quenched martensite on nucleation kinetics of subsequent bainite transformation and agree that the pre-quenched martensite can accelerate subsequent bainite nucleation. Navarro-López et al. [ 16 ] reported that the nucleation of bainite ferrite at below Ms is at least two orders of magnitude faster than above Ms due to the presence of pre-quenched martensite. Ravi et al. [ 17 ] suggested that the acceleration of bainite transformation in the presence of pre-quenched martensite is due to the nucleation of bainite begins simultaneously at both austenite grain boundaries as well as martensite/austenite interfaces. However, in view of the bainite transformation after martensite pre-quenching include nucleation and growth stage, few studies pay attention to the effect of martensite pre-quenching on bainite growth. Kawata et al. [ 18 ] suggested that more pre-quenched martensite fraction could further accelerate subsequent bainite transformation due to the increasing of nucleation sites at the interfaces of pre-quenched martensite/austenite. Li et al. [ 19 ] argue that the more fraction of pre-quenched martenite is not beneficial to nucleate for subsequent bainite transformation. On the other hand, Sourmail et al. [ 20 ] point out that pre-quenched martensite could shorten the overall heat treatment time but have no detectable acceleration in subsequent bainite transformation. Therefore, it is important to investigate the effect of pre-quenched martensite on the growth of subsequent bainite transformation which is critical to determine the mechanical properties of martensite-bainite duplex steel.

As discussed above, although the pre-quenched martensite is beneficial to nucleate of subsequent bainite transformation, however, the effect of pre-quenched martensite on the growth of bainite transformation remains dispute. Meanwhile, the effect of pre-quenched martensite on retained austenite stability of GCr15 bearing steel has not been explored, which is a key factor to determine the dimensional stability of bearings. Thus, the aim of this study is to investigate the effect of pre-quenched martensite on the growth stage of subsequent bainite transformation of GCr15 bearing steel. Additionally, the effect of pre-quenched martensite on the evolution of martensite-bainite duplex microstructures, strength-toughness and retained austenite stability are also discussing.

sections.heading: Dilatometry observation and mechanical properties
paragraphs:
The GCr15 bearing steel was supplied as spheroidization annealed condition with the nominal composition of Fe-1.05C-0.27Si-1.46Cr-0.33Mn-0.002 P (wt.%). The Bähr DIL805A dilatometer was used to study the effect of pre-quenched martensite on subsequent bainite transformation kinetics. Dilatometric specimens were machined parallel to rolling direction by wire-electrode with a size of φ 4 × 10 mm. Specimens were placed between two quartz rods, heating by an induction coil and using nitrogen gas to cool. A thermocouple was spot-welded in the middle of specimens to control temperature. The Ms temperature was measured to be 232 °C by dilatometric curve as shown in  Fig. 1 
                         a, which the specimen was austenitizing at 850 °C for 15 min with a heating rate of 5 °C/s and then cooling down to room temperature with a cooling rate of 30 °C/s. The heating and cooling parameters of martensite pre-quenching and subsequent bainite transformation process are present in  Fig. 1 b. For comparison, the direct bainite austempering at 240 °C was also conducted.

The different heat treatment procedures are shown in  Table 1 
                         , conventional QT (Procedure E) and direct bainite austempering heat treatment (Procedure F) are conduct to as reference. Standard tensile tests were conducted on a Zwick/Roell Z100 universal testing machine with a strain rate of 2 × 10 −3  s −1  at room temperature and the gauge length was set to 16 mm. Strain and stress were measured by an extensometer and a force sensor, respectively. The impact toughness of un-notched specimens was evaluated by charpy test with standard dimensions of 10 × 10 × 55 mm. The strength and impact toughness is average values of three tests. The hardness was measured using the Rockwell hardness tester with a load of 150 kg.

sections.heading: Microstructures observation and quantitative characterization
paragraphs: The heat treated specimens were metallographically prepared by grinding and polishing up to 0.5 μm. Then, the 3% Nital was applied for etching specimens to observe microstructures by optical microscopy (OM, ZEISS AxidoCam MRC5) and scanning electron microscope (SEM, JEOL, 6500F) equipped with an electron backscattered diffraction (EBSD) detector. The specimens for EBSD observe were vibratory polished with colloidal silica after mechanical polishing to 0.5 μm. Specimens for transmission electron microscopy (TEM, JEOL, 2100 F) were prepared by a twin-jet polisher using 4% perchloric acid and 96% ethanol at room temperature with an applied potential of 40 V.

Specimens for magnetic measurements were cut by wire-electrode with a size of φ 5 × 2 mm and measured with a Quantum Design Physical Property Measurement System (PPMS-9T (EC-II)). The applied magnetic field is change from 5 T to 0 T in steps of 0.25 T at room temperature. Then the  f

Ms( c ) and Ms( f ) are determined by the fitting tested magnetic curves. The as-received material was austenitizing at 900 °C for 30min, fast cooling to 780 °C and then slow cooling to 650 °C, finally air cooling to room temperature for obtain the austenite-free specimen. In addition, the carbon content in retained austenite was calculated by using XRD lattice parameters obtained from γ (220)  peak.

The bainite in the microstructures is revealed by Lepera's etching agent [ 23 , 24 ] and the fraction of bainite ( f 
                         B ) was measured by net-point counting method with an average from five visual fields by combines OM with Image-pro plus software. The polished specimen with freshly surfaces etched in a 10% aqueous solution of sodium metabisulphite for 10～15 s. The specimen should be oscillated during etching and immediately flushed with ethanol and dried using cool air flow. The specimen is observed with a microscope equipped with a high-brightness halogen lamp. For optimal contrast in light microscopy, the aperture iris diaphragm must be carefully adjusted to allow clear distinction of different phases.

sections.heading: Mechanical stability of retained austenite
paragraphs: Retained austenite is a metastable phase in microstructures at room temperature, which will be transform to martensite under external applied stress when bearings during operating condition and causes dimensional change, which is the most important issue for high precision parts and components, such as aerospace industry and precision machine tools [ 25 , 26 ]. Therefore, it is important to investigate the mechanical stability of retained austenite in GCr15 bearing steel.

To investigate the mechanical stability of retained austenite, the 10% compressive strain was conducted to specimens using a Zwick/Roell Z100 universal testing machine with strain rate of 2 × 10 −3  s −1  at room temperature. Each heat treated specimen was cut into a column with a size of φ5 × 10 mm by wire-electrode. Before and after compressive strain, the fraction of retained austenite is calculating by magnetic measurements. Then, the mechanical stability of retained austenite can be evaluated by the exponential decay law which proposed by Sugimoto et al. [ 27 ]：

sections.heading: Effect of martensite pre-quenching on subsequent bainite transformation
paragraphs:
The dilatometric curves in  Fig. 2 
                         a present martensite pre-quenching at 220, 200, 180, 160 °C and subsequent bainite transformation at 240 °C, and direct bainite austempering at 240 °C, respectively. The initial contraction of curves from austenitizing condition is due to temperature change from 850 °C to different martensite pre-quenching and austempering temperatures. The following increase of dilatometric curves is the results of pre-quenched martensite formed. It can be seen that the dilatometric curves clearly increased with the decreasing of pre-quenching temperature. After 5 min holding at pre-quenching temperature, the dilatometric curves sharply increase when heating to 240 °C. Then, the following increase of dilatometric curves are attribute to bainite transformation. The slope of dilatometric curves after holding 7200 s at 240 °C was close to zero indicate that bainite transformation is complete.  Fig. 2 b shows the bainite fraction formed after different martensite pre-quenching temperatures and direct austempering as a function of isothermal holding time at 240 °C, which is assume that all austenite transforms to bainite after isothermal holding 7200 s except for undissolved spherical carbides. The austempering specimen at 240 °C obtained the maximum bainite fraction, but decreases with the decreasing of martensite pre-quenching temperatures, which is due to the lower martensite pre-quenching temperature, the higher fraction of pre-quenched martensite. It seems that the bainite transformation during direct austempering in the initial stage is slower than that of after martensite pre-quenching.

Fig. 2 c shows the bainite transformation rate after different martensite pre-quenching temperature and direct bainite austempering at 240 °C, respectively. In the direct bainite austempering specimen, there is an obviously platform which bainite transformation rate equal to zero. In contrast, the bainite transformation rate in all martensite pre-quenching specimens are direct increasing during bainite isothermal holding. This result confirms that bainite transformation in direct austempering has longer incubation period than that of martensite pre-quenching. In other words, martensite pre-quenching has significantly accelerate effect on the nucleation of subsequent bainite transformation. Meanwhile, martensite pre-quenching at 200 °C has the shortest incubation period of subsequent bainite transformation. Moreover, the transformation rate of bainite in martensite pre-quenching specimen in the initial growth stage is faster than direct bainite austempering specimen, and decreased with the decreasing of martensite pre-quenching temperature. This result indicates that the more fraction of pre-quenched martensite is not beneficial to subsequent bainite nucleation and growth, which is due to bainite transformation after martensite pre-quenching bear more complicated stresses with increasing fraction of pre-quenched martensite [ 28 , 29 ].

The more detailed comparison of growth stage of bainite transformation after martensite pre-quenching at 200 °C and direct bainite austempering at 240 °C is shown in  Fig. 2 d. The bainite growth follows an S-shape curve during direct bainite austempering at 240 °C. However, the curve changes from S-shape curve to an initial rapidly ascending curve in martensite pre-quenching specimen. The table inserted in  Fig. 2 d also shows that the fraction of bainite at 240 °C for 250s and 500s is 13% and 28.6% after martensite pre-quenching at 200 °C, which is higher than that of 3.5% and 22.9% during direct bainite austempering at 240 °C. This result indicates that in the initial growth stage of bainite transformation after martensite pre-quenching is faster than direct bainite austempering at 240 °C. However, the fraction of bainite at 240 °C for 750s is 38.3% after martensite pre-quenching at 200 °C is lower than that of 47.1% during direct bainite austempering at 240 °C. Combing with transformation rate in  Fig. 2 c, this results further illustrate that the pre-quenched martensite is strongly accelerate nucleate and initial growth of subsequent bainite transformation.

sections.heading: Microstructures observation
paragraphs:
Fig. 3 
                          present the microstructures of heat-treated specimens of conventional QT, austempering and martensite pre-quenching, respectively. The typical microstructures after conventional QT treatment was shown in  Fig. 3 a, which is consist of tempered martensite, a few of RA and undissolved spherical carbides. The exist of undissolved spherical carbides in microstructures is beneficial to fatigue and wear behavior of bearings during applications [ 30 , 31 ]. However, the precipitated transition carbides in tempered martensite can barely be distinguished by SEM.  Fig. 3 b shows the microstructures after austempering at 240 °C for 4 h, which is mainly consist of bainite, undissolved spherical carbides and a few of retained austenite.

Fig. 3 c～f shows the microstructures of different martensite pre-quenching at 220, 200, 180 and 160 °C for 5 min and subsequent bainite transformation at 240 °C for 18 min, respectively. The microstructures are the mixture of pre-quenched martensite, bainite, retained austenite, althermal martensite and undissolved spherical carbides. The pre-quenched martensite is mainly formed as lath-shaped structures which will be tempered during subsequent isothermal holding at 240 °C and precipitate multi-directional transition carbides. The bainite ferrite grows nearby the pre-quenched martensite which is maintains a similar crystallographic orientation relationship [ 32 ]. The formation of althermal martensite indicates that bainite transformation is incomplete after holding at 240 °C for 18 min, and martensite transformation occurs during oil quenching and leaves small blocky irregular-shaped M/A islands in the final microstructures. Retained austenite is presented as two different morphologies [ 13 ], one is appears as film-like, the other is in the form of small elongated blocky.

The fraction of constituent phase in microstructures is shown in  Table 2 
                         . It can be seen that with martensite pre-quenching temperature decrease, the fraction of pre-quenched martensite increasing from 16.5% at 220 °C to 61.5% at 160 °C and the fraction of bainite is decreasing from 45.8% to 9.2%. Although more pre-quenched martensite may produce more nucleation sites, at the same time, it also consumes a large amount of austenite. Therefore, the subsequent bainite growth at 240 °C may be hinder by the exist of surrounded pre-quenched martnesite [ 33 ]. After incomplete bainite transformation at 240 °C for 18min, the remaining austenite will partly transform to althermal martensite during oil quenching. The more retained austenite and less althermal martensite will leave in room temperature microstructures with decreasing of martensite pre-quenching temperatures, which is attribute to the more fraction of pre-quenched martensite may increases the stability of austenite due to carbon partitioning during isothermal holding at 240 °C and constrained by surrounded harder phase, such as pre-quenched martensite and bainite.

sections.heading: Strength and toughness
paragraphs:
The strength, hardness and impact toughness of heat treated specimens of conventional QT, austempering and martensite pre-quenching are list in  Table 3 
                         , respectively. It can be seen that the QT heat treated specimen has the highest tensile strength and hardness values of 2170Mpa and 62.5HRC, the austempering specimen has the lowest tensile strength and hardness values of 1940Mpa and 58HRC, receptively. Although the hardness value of martensite pre-quenching specimens lower than that of QT treated specimen, however, they all higher than 59 HRC and satisfy the needs of bearing applications. Meanwhile, the impact toughness of martensite pre-quenching specimens at 200 °C reach to 71 J, which is obviously higher than that of QT heat treated specimen and equivalent to austempering specimen. In other words, the specimen of martensite pre-quenching specimen at 200 °C has the optimal combination of strength and toughness. Therefore, this results demonstrate that combining martensite pre-quenching and subsequent bainite transformation could have better combination of strength and toughness than that of single conventional QT treatment or austempering.

Fig. 4 
                          show the SEM fractographs of impact specimens treated by conventional QT, austempering and martensite pre-quenching, respectively. The fractured surface present as quasi-cleavage fracture and tear ridges are also visible. It is should be notice that many undissolved spherical carbide particles and microvoids can be observed in the fracture surface, which indicates that microcracks nucleate between spherical carbides and matrix during impact test. Microvoids is the residual traces of undissolved spherical carbides particles fallen off during impact test. The fractograph in  Fig. 4 a shows obvious flat facets after QT treatment. However, there is exists dimples after austempering at 240 °C for 4 h, as shown in  Fig. 4 b. Moreover,  Fig. 4 c shows the more obvious tearing ridges and dimples are present in the martensite-bainite duplex microstructures indicates the specimen had already conducted to a certain amount of plastic deformation when fracture occurred. This results indirectly demonstrates that the martensite-bainite duplex microstructures have better impact toughness than that of single martensite.

Fig. 5 
                         a and b show the distribution of boundary misorientation angle in specimen heat-treated by QT and martensite pre-quenching at 200 °C. It can be seen that the relative frequency of low angle boundaries (<10°) from 38% in QT specimen significantly increases to 69% in martensite pre-quenching at 200 °C specimen. Wang [ 34 , 35 ] has reported that the increased effective boundaries can strongly hinder fracture cracks propagation, and thereby improve impact toughness. In this study, the higher fraction of low angle boundaries obtained in martensite pre-quenching at 200 °C and bainite transformation at 240 °C specimen is mainly attribute to the multi-stage phase transformation. Firstly, the formation of pre-quenched martensite could partitioning the prior austenite and reduce the size of untransformed blocky austenite. Secondly, bainite is prone to form at lower carbon area and further partitioning untransformed blocky austenite during subsequent bainite transformation at 240 °C. Meanwhile, the carbon atoms in pre-quenched martensite could diffuse into austenite (untransformed during pre-quenching), thereby stabilizing a portion of austenite (especially those adjacent to pre-quenched martensite). Finally, the untransformed blocky austenite after bainite transformation at 240 °C for 18min could further partitioning by martensite transformation during oil quenching to room temperature. Therefore, this multi-stage phase transformation can obviously partition austenite and refine martensite-bainite duplex microstructures to produce a great deal of low angle boundaries.

sections.heading: Mechanical stability of retained austenite
paragraphs:
Fig. 6 
                          show the magnetic curves for calculate the fraction of retained austenite by magnetic method before and after compression, respectively. The calculated fraction of retained austenite and the mechanical stability of  K  value are list in  Table 4 
                         . It is notice that the fraction of retained austenite in direct austempering specimen is just 3.2% so that its influence on mechanical stability is thought to be insignificant. The fraction of retained austenite increases with the decreasing of martensite pre-quenching temperatures. However, all the  K  value in martensite pre-quenching specimens is lower than that of QT treated specimen and increases with the decreasing of marteniste pre-quenching temperatures, which means that all martensite pre-queching specimen obtained higher mechanical stability of retained austenite than QT specimen. Additionally, the mechanical stability of retained austenite decreasing with the decrease of martensite pre-quenching temperature.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs:
The effect of pre-quenched martensite on subsequent bainite transformation kinetics, martensite/bainite duplex microstructures, strength-toughness and retained austenite stability of GCr15 bearing steel were investigated. The main conclusions can be summarized as following: 
                         
                            1. 
                            Martensite pre-quenching is obviously accelerate nucleation of subsequent bainite transformation in comparison to direct bainite austempering. However, the more fraction of pre-quenched martensite, the lower transformation rate of subsequent bainite nucleation and growth. 
                         
                         
                            2. 
                            Excellent combination of strength-toughness of GCr15 bearing steel obtained by martensite pre-quenching at 200 °C, which has more than 35% volume fraction of bainite, is mainly attribute to the large amounts of low angle boundaries (<10°) produced by multi-stage phase transformation. 
                         
                         
                            3. 
                            The mechanical stability of retained austenite in all martennsite pre-quenching specimen is higher than that of QT specimen, which is due to the formation of film-like morphology and carbon enriched retained austenite.
